---
title: "7.3 Nominal X Continuous Interactions"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

- Nominal X Continuous interactions are perhaps the prototypical interaction effect (and the examples above show: separate prediction lines where each line represents a different group)
  - Plots are the most effective way to show these
- Do not use the coefficient on the interaction (product) term as the test of interaction
  - Must use the 1^st^ and 2^nd^ difference approach for all **nonlinear** models (including nonlinear effects with linear regression)
    - Absent a theoretically important region of your data, average effects are appropriate
    - But remember that the effects will vary in other regions of the data---always test for interaction where it is most relevant for your research question

## Why you should ignore the β coefficients when testing nonlinear interaction effects

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/doan_love_SF", clear

*Binary DV: support for legal marriage model
logit Bmarry i.cond##c.love10 rfem age rce_wht ed_coll ///
    ed_hs inc_50k married childyn children ideo evangel ///
    mainline blackprot catholic ofaithV2, or
est store marry
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

```{r}
library(haven)           # import Stata data and labels
library(dplyr)           # data manipulation
library(ggplot2)         # graphs
library(modelsummary)    # regression tables
library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects
library(cleanplots)      # graph scheme
cleanplots_defaults()

love <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/doan_love_SF.dta")

# Keep model variables; drop any missing data
love <- love[c("Bmarry", "cond", "love10", "rfem", "age", "rce_wht", "ed_coll",
  "ed_hs", "inc_50k", "married", "childyn", "children", "ideo", "evangel",
  "mainline", "blackprot", "catholic", "ofaithV2")]
love <- love[complete.cases(love), ] |>
  mutate(cond = as_factor(cond))

# Binary DV: support for legal marriage model
marry <- glm(Bmarry ~ cond * love10 + rfem + age + rce_wht + ed_coll + ed_hs +
  inc_50k + married + childyn + children + ideo + evangel + mainline + blackprot +
  catholic + ofaithV2, data = love, family = binomial(link = "logit"))

modelsummary(marry, exponentiate = TRUE, stars = c("*" = .05, "**" = .01, "***" = .001),
  coef_omit = "rfem|age|rce_wht|ed_|inc_50k|married|child|ideo|evangel|mainline|blackprot|catholic|ofaith")
```

:::

- If we approached the interaction effect from this nonlinear model as we would for linear effects, the conclusion would be that: *the effect of love is no different for gay and lesbian couples, compared to the effect of love for heterosexual couple*

  **This is wrong.**

### Plot the predictions

- The presence of interaction terms in the model does not change the code for plotting predictions at all

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

- In Stata, use **margins** for the predictions and **marginsplot** to make the graph

```stata
margins cond, at(love10=(0(0.5)10))

marginsplot
```

## R

- In R, use **plot_predictions**

```r
plot_predictions(marry, by = c("love10", "cond"),
  newdata = datagrid(love10 = seq(0, 10, .5), cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
mtable, at(love10=(0 10) cond=(1 2 3)) decimals(2)

*7.3.a
qui margins, at(love10=(0(0.5)10) cond=(1 2 3))
marginsplot, recastci(rline) ciopt(lpat(dash) lcol(*.3)) xlab(0(2)10) ylab(0(.2)1.1) ///
    title("[7.3.a] Pred Prob of Supporting Legal Marriage by Perceptions of Love", size(medium)) ///
    subtitle("Effect of Sexual Orientation of Couple") ///
    ytitle("Pr(Support Marriage)") xtitle("Perceptions of Love") ///
    text(1.03 .5 "Pr = .97"  1.05 9.5 "Pr = .99", size(small) color(red*1.2)) ///
    text(0.05 .5 "Pr = .10"  0.87 9.5 "Pr = .79", size(small) color(eltblue)) ///
    text(0.49 .5 "Pr = .37"  0.58 9.5 "Pr = .71", size(small) color(gs6))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_03_a-love.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_03_a-love.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.3.a] Predicted probability of supporting legal marriage by perceptions of love (0 to 10) for heterosexual, gay, and lesbian couples. Support for heterosexual couples is nearly flat near the top, from .97 to .99. Support for gay couples rises steeply from .10 to .79, and for lesbian couples from .37 to .71; the gay and lesbian lines cross near love = 8."}

## R

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.3.a] Predicted probability of supporting legal marriage by perceptions of love (0 to 10) for heterosexual, gay, and lesbian couples. Support for heterosexual couples is nearly flat near the top, from .97 to .99. Support for gay couples rises steeply from .10 to .79, and for lesbian couples from .37 to .71; the gay and lesbian lines cross near love = 8."
avg_predictions(marry, by = c("love10", "cond"),
  newdata = datagrid(love10 = c(0, 10), cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))

# 7.3.a
plot_predictions(marry, by = c("love10", "cond"),
  newdata = datagrid(love10 = seq(0, 10, .5), cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) +
  annotate("text", x = c(.5, 9.5, .5, 9.5, .5, 9.5), y = c(1.03, 1.05, .05, .87, .49, .58),
    label = c("Pr = .97", "Pr = .99", "Pr = .10", "Pr = .79", "Pr = .37", "Pr = .71"),
    size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10, 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, .2)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1.1)) +
  labs(title = "[7.3.a] Pred Prob of Supporting Legal Marriage by Perceptions of Love",
    subtitle = "Effect of Sexual Orientation of Couple",
    x = "Perceptions of Love", y = "Pr(Support Marriage)", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

## Calculating 2^nd^ differences in Stata and R

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

- In Stata, use [**mecompare**](/software/mecompare/examples/model-types.qmd) to calculate marginal effects of a focal IV (in the *varlist*) **by( )** levels of the moderating variable
  - [Go here for several examples of using **mecompare** for interactions](/software/mecompare/interactions/index.qmd)

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
// MEs (1st differences) with mecompare.
**Focal IV goes in varlist; moderating variable in by( )
mecompare love10, by(cond) model(marry)
<</dd_do>>
```

- Use **metest** for the 2^nd^ difference: equality of any two MEs (1^st^ differences)
  - Refer to ME \# from **mecompare** table

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*use metest for 2nd difference: equality of any two MEs
metest 2 - 1
<</dd_do>>
```

- Can accumulate tests into a single table with **metest**

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*Accumulate all 2nd diffs into a single metest table
metest, clear
qui metest 2 - 1, add rowname("Gay - Hetero")
qui metest 3 - 1, add rowname("Lesbian - Hetero")
qui metest 2 - 3, add rowname("Gay - Lesbian")
metest, title("2nd difference of effect of love, by couple type")
<</dd_do>>
```

## R

- In R, use **avg_comparisons** to calculate the MEs (1^st^ differences)

```{r}
# Changes in continuous IVs centered on the observed values, like mecompare
options(marginaleffects_contrast_direction = "center")

# MEs (1st differences)
avg_comparisons(marry, variables = "love10", by = "cond",
  newdata = datagrid(cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"))
```

- Add a **hypothesis** option to test for 2^nd^ difference (the equality of any two MEs)
  - MEs named **b#** in order they appear in **avg_comparisons** output from last step

```{r}
avg_comparisons(marry, variables = "love10", by = "cond",
  newdata = datagrid(cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  hypothesis = "b2 - b1 = 0")
```

- The hypothesis option \~pairwise will calculate all 2^nd^ differences

```{r}
avg_comparisons(marry, variables = "love10", by = "cond",
  newdata = datagrid(cond = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual"),
  hypothesis = ~ pairwise)
```

:::

> *The effect of love is stronger for gay couples than for heterosexual couples, indicating an interaction effect (2^nd^ diff. = 0.068, p \< .001).*

> *Etc.*

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
See additional example interpretations under "Example write-up" below
:::

## Plotting the "other side" of the interaction

- Conceptually, it is useful to specify a focal IV and a moderating IV
  - This is mostly a theoretical distinction, but can influence the test with nonlinearities
- Usually, the variable that comes first in your research question/hypothesis is the focal IV; the variable whose effect it (may) vary across is the moderating IV

> ***RQ ex**: Do perceptions of love have different effects for varying couple types?*
>
> ***H ex**: Perceptions of love should have a stronger effect for gay couples compared to its effect for heterosexual couples.*

> ***RQ ex**: Does aging lead to declining physical health at equal rates for individuals from different racial-ethnic backgrounds?*
>
> ***H ex**: Aging will have a stronger (more negative) effect on physical health for Black than for White adults.*

- The examples above focus mostly on the effect of love as the focal IV, and couple type as the moderating IV
- It is also important to examine the effect of the moderating IV, across values of the focal IV
  - Essentially, flip the focal and moderating variable
- For a continuous X nominal interaction: calculate the marginal effect (ME) of the nominal IV across the range of the continuous IV and plot it
  - Note for this example because our nominal IV has 3 categories we have to pick a reference category and then plot two lines which are the differences from the reference

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

- In Stata, calculate ME of nominal IV across range of continuous IV using **margins**
  - Plot with **marginsplot**

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
*7.3.b - Effect of sexual orientation (heterosexual vs [gay & lesbian])
*   over range of love
est restore marry

qui margins, dydx(cond) at(love=(0(0.5)10))

marginsplot, recastci(rline) ci1opts(lpat(dash) col(eltblue*.4)) ///
    ci2opts(lpat(dash) col(gs10*.4)) ///
    plot1op(lcol(eltblue) msym(none) lwid(medthick)) ///
    plot2op(lcol(gs10) msym(none) lwid(medthick)) ///
    ylab(-1(0.2)0.2) xlab(0(1)10) yline(0, lcol(black)) ///
    title("[7.3.b] Difference in Support for Marriage: Gay/Lesbian vs Heterosexual Couple", size(medsmall)) ///
    subtitle("Effects Below Zero Indicate Lower Support for Gay/Lesbian Couple's Marriage Rights", size(small)) ///
    ytitle("Pr(Support): Gay/Lesbian - Heterosexual") ///
    legend(order(3 "Gay vs Hetero" 4 "Lesbian vs Hetero") pos(6) row(1))
<</dd_do>>
<<dd_do: quietly>>
graph export "fig/cda-07_03_b-love.png", replace width(1400)
<</dd_do>>
```

![](fig/cda-07_03_b-love.png){width=80% fig-alt="[7.3.b] Marginal effect of couple type (gay vs heterosexual and lesbian vs heterosexual) on the probability of supporting marriage, across perceptions of love from 0 to 10, with confidence intervals and a line at zero. Both differences are negative throughout: the gay vs heterosexual difference rises from about -0.87 at love = 0 to about -0.2 at love = 10, and the lesbian vs heterosexual difference rises from about -0.6 to about -0.28; the lines cross near love = 8."}

## R

- In R, use **plot_comparisons**

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "[7.3.b] Marginal effect of couple type (gay vs heterosexual and lesbian vs heterosexual) on the probability of supporting marriage, across perceptions of love from 0 to 10, with confidence intervals and a line at zero. Both differences are negative throughout: the gay vs heterosexual difference rises from about -0.87 at love = 0 to about -0.2 at love = 10, and the lesbian vs heterosexual difference rises from about -0.6 to about -0.28; the lines cross near love = 8."
# 7.3.b - Effect of sexual orientation (heterosexual vs [gay & lesbian])
#   over range of love (MEs saved and passed to ggplot to draw both lines in one panel)
mes <- avg_comparisons(marry, variables = "cond", by = c("love10", "contrast"),
  newdata = datagrid(love10 = seq(0, 10, .5), grid_type = "counterfactual"))

ggplot(mes, aes(x = love10, y = estimate, color = contrast, fill = contrast)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high), alpha = .2, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#8FC6EB", "#909090"),
    labels = c("Gay vs Hetero", "Lesbian vs Hetero")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#8FC6EB", "#909090"),
    labels = c("Gay vs Hetero", "Lesbian vs Hetero")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(-1, .2, .2)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-1, .2)) +
  labs(title = "[7.3.b] Difference in Support for Marriage: Gay/Lesbian vs Heterosexual Couple",
    subtitle = "Effects Below Zero Indicate Lower Support for Gay/Lesbian Couple's Marriage Rights",
    x = "How in love?", y = "Pr(Support): Gay/Lesbian - Heterosexual", color = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

:::

\*Recall this is a direct test of gay vs heterosexual couple: if the 95% confidence interval does not overlap zero: the group difference is statistically significant at *p* \< 0.05

## Example write-up

> *Perceptions of how in love a couple is have differential effects on how supportive someone is of legal marriage rights, depending on the sexual orientation of the couple. For heterosexual couples, perceptions of love have no effect on support for marriage (∆~heterosexual~ p = ns). This is because heterosexual couples receive overwhelming support for legal marriage regardless of whether someone sees them as not in love at all (Pr = 0.97) or whether they see them as extremely in love (Pr = 0.99; see red line in Figure 1). Perceptions of love have a relatively small but significant effect on support for marriage of lesbian couples (∆~lesbian~ = 0.033 p \< 0.05). There is a large positive effect of love for gay couples (∆~gay~ = 0.071 p \< 0.001). For example, support for legal marriage rises drastically over the range of love, from a low of just 0.10 to a high of 0.79 for gay couples who are viewed as extremely in love (see blue line in Figure 1). The effect of love is stronger for gay men than for heterosexual couples (2^nd^ difference = 0.068; p \< 0.001) and for gay men compared to lesbian couples (2^nd^ difference = 0.037; p \< 0.05). However, it is important to note that despite the strong increase in support for marriage for gay couples as perceptions of love increase, support for a gay couple's marriage rights is never equal to support for heterosexual couple's marriage rights (see Figure 2).*

![](images/petts-kaufman-mize-2023-predictions.png){width=48% fig-alt="Figure 1 from Petts, Kaufman, and Mize (2023): perceptions of an employee as a good parent by weeks of leave offered, for fathers and mothers. Both curves rise and then fall, peaking around 9 to 11 weeks."} ![](images/petts-kaufman-mize-2023-marginal-effects.png){width=48% fig-alt="Figure 3 from Petts, Kaufman, and Mize (2023): the marginal effect of parental gender (mothers minus fathers) across weeks of leave offered, with confidence intervals and a line at zero. The effect dips slightly below zero in the middle weeks and rises above zero at the longest leaves."}

\*I like including both graphs in a single paper (often as separate panels) to help the reader follow what the second graph shows. Example from [Petts, Kaufman, and Mize 2023](https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.12875)
